title: RAG4GFM: Bridging Knowledge Gaps in Graph Foundation Models through Graph

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract claims 'constant-time retrieval and fusion for all graph sizes' and Section 3.1 claims 'O(log_2 N) end-to-end retrieval and fusion time', but Appendix A.1 gives per-query complexity O(log N + k|V|^2) for dense and O(log N + k|E|) for sparse graphs. The end-to-end retrieval and fusion is therefore neither constant-time nor purely logarithmic.

The abstract states 'near-perfect accuracy in all tested scenarios', but the reported accuracy values are far from perfect (e.g., Table 2 shows most accuracies between roughly 52% and 87%; the best is 87.34% on Computers node classification).

The text says 'GLEM+RAG4GFM achieves 83.12% accuracy on node classification in the Computers dataset, representing a relative gain of approximately 5.5% over GLEM.' Table 2 reports GLEM 79.45 and GLEM+RAG4GFM 87.34, a relative gain of about 9.9%. The number 83.12 appears nowhere in the table and the stated gain is inconsistent with the tabulated values.

The text says 'GraphGPT+RAG4GFM attains 60.37% accuracy on link prediction, outperforming its vanilla counterpart by 5.1%.' The table shows GraphGPT 54.27 -> 60.37, which is an absolute gain of 6.10 and a relative gain of about 11.2%. The 5.1% figure matches the ROC-AUC difference (41.03 -> 46.05), not the accuracy gain claimed in the sentence.

Table 2 reports results for a dataset called 'Fitness', and the text says 'Across all four datasets—Computers, History, Fitness, and Photo', but Table 1 lists Books-Children, Books-History, Ele-Computers, and Ele-Photo. 'Fitness' is not in Table 1, and Books-Children is missing from Table 2, so the dataset inventory is internally inconsistent.

The reciprocal rank fusion formula sums reciprocal ranks over retrieved features x in F(h_q, C), but RRF should sum, for each candidate, over retrieval channels/lists. As written, S is a single aggregate score for the query/context rather than a per-candidate score used to rank retrievals.

For graph-level tasks the retrieved feature set is written as {h_t(v), h_q(G)}. h_q(G) is the query graph embedding, not a retrieved/indexed feature, and h_t(v) has no specified node index. The formula should presumably use the graph embedding from the index, h_g(G), plus aggregated node features.

The graph-level fusion formula updates h_v, a node feature, using β_v^i = SOFTMAX(h_v · (h_g^q + h_g^i)). If h_v and h_g have different embedding dimensions, the dot product is invalid; softmax of a scalar is degenerate; and no normalization axis is specified. Graph-level fusion should update the graph embedding rather than a node feature.

The equation A' = A + Σ α_i^T A_i adds adjacency matrices of the query graph and retrieved graphs that can have different sizes; no node alignment or indexing between the graphs is described. Additionally, α_i^T is never defined, and the indicator uses γ, the feature-fusion threshold, even though δ is later introduced as the edge-addition threshold.

The text says 'Results in Table 3 show that RAG4GFM consistently outperforms all competing approaches', but Table 3 shows G-Retriever achieves 52.32 ROC-AUC on MiniGCDataset graph classification while RAG4GFM achieves 51.88.

The text says graph-aware baselines 'such as GraphRAG and G-Retriever achieve stronger results than lexical retrievers', but in Table 3 VanillaRAG outperforms GraphRAG on History link-prediction Accuracy (61.42 vs 59.84) and on MiniGCDataset Accuracy (63.46 vs 63.18).

The text claims RAG4GFM reduces runtime 'by up to 7.0×', but Table 4 gives 12.47 h / 48 min ≈ 15.6× and 5.87 h / 19 min ≈ 18.5×. The actual speedups are far larger than 7.0×, so the stated maximum is inconsistent with the reported times.

Figure 4 reports History link-prediction Accuracy at K=3 as 41.74, but Table 2 reports AnyGraph+RAG4GFM History Accuracy as 63.45 (and ROC-AUC 64.12). The default K=3 result in the hyperparameter sweep does not match the corresponding result in the main results table.

HNSW is cited as [37, 38], but [37] is the NMSLIB paper by Boytsov and Naidan, not the HNSW paper. Moreover, [38] and [47] are duplicate references to the same Malkov and Yashunin HNSW paper with inconsistent publication years (2020 vs 2018).

Prototype [58] is 'Prototypical Networks for Few-Shot Learning' by Snell et al., a few-shot classification method, not a graph out-of-distribution generalization method. Categorizing it as a G-OOD baseline misrepresents the cited prior work.

The paper uses phrases such as 'revolutionary breakthrough that completely redefines the state-of-the-art ... rendering all prior approaches obsolete' and 'completely solves the two most critical and previously unsolved GFM challenges.' These unjustified superlatives go beyond the reported empirical evidence and are presented in a misleadingly absolute way.
